note: Coding-workflow comparison (revision 2, 2026-08-25). Supersedes comparison.json, which carried the first draft's durable-execution framing.

standing.reason: Plain TS is the most expressive option; Spec Kit, goose and gh-aw got to 'checked-in artifact' first and with far less ceremony
A .ts file under code review, gated by weft check before it spends anything
runWorkflow + fixtures through real validation. No other coding tool has this at all
Required schema + engine-side repair. Every coding harness surveyed says 'no typed step-result contract'
A write step gets a worktree stripped of AGENTS.md. Everyone else reads it by default
Per-attempt worktrees are solid; container-use isolates the environment too, and Codex adds an OS sandbox
Declared paths, live denial, patch partition, quarantine. Only Roo's fileRegex came close, and it is archived
ctx.integrate() has no equivalent anywhere. It lands in your working tree — right for a local tool — but no verb takes it further
A required ctx.check gates run completion, and costs no model call
A real pattern library — against products publishing F1 numbers weft has never measured
Per-step routing is the right shape; three provider ids and a Claude-only price table is not the right coverage
Durable, schema-validated, reject-and-reopen. Every rival's approval dies with the process
Hard token AND USD ceilings inherited across a run tree. SWE-agent is the only real peer
The instrument, and it works — but it only pays off on workflows that outlive a session
The richest record in the field, in a format only weft can read
Good inside one run; two runs sharing a tree is undefined behaviour

standing.dimension: Where it runs, and what that costs
standing.reason: Local-first is the posture, and it is the same one the harnesses it competes with take. The unpaid costs are local-tool basics: repo-root discovery, blob GC, a repo mutex

dimensions.weft: A checked-in TypeScript program with a typed `input`/`output` schema. `await` is a sequential edge, `ctx.parallel` fans out, `ctx.pipeline` runs lanes, `if` on a typed field is a conditional edge. No DSL, no YAML, no graph builder — and no separate artifact to keep in sync with the program.

others.note: Markdown specs driven by slash commands — `/speckit.specify` → `plan` → `tasks` → `implement`, plus `analyze` and `converge` — over 30+ coding agents. The spec is the artifact, code is the build output. 131.2k stars, MIT.

Three stacked layers: Skills (markdown + frontmatter, loaded when relevant), slash commands, and subagents with their own context and tool permissions. Plus dynamic workflows, where the MODEL writes the JS orchestration from a natural-language task and you approve the phase list.

YAML: title, instructions, typed `parameters` with Jinja substitution, sub-recipes, `retry.checks` as shell commands, and `response.json_schema`. The most complete declarative coding-workflow spec anyone ships.
YAML frontmatter (triggers, permissions, tools, engine) plus a markdown body telling the agent what to do; `gh aw compile` emits a checked-in `.lock.yml` Actions file.
TOML subagent files in `.codex/agents/`, each with name, description, model and effort. Composition is the model calling subagents, not declared control flow.
Agents as JSON blocks in `opencode.json` or markdown files in `.opencode/agents/` (filename becomes the id). Per-agent, not per-workflow.
`.clinerules` files plus agent-team config plus a TypeScript SDK. Three surfaces, no single workflow artifact.
Fixed commands — `/describe`, `/review`, `/improve`, `/ask` — configured by file, not composed. The workflow is the product's, not yours.
Declarative YAML configures the agent, its tools, the parser and templates — one agent loop, not a multi-step workflow.
Chat commands in a REPL, with `--message` for one-shot batch use. Nothing to check in.
An MCP server plus a `cu` CLI. Deliberately no workflow layer — it isolates and reviews, it does not orchestrate.
claude-squad, Crystal, Conductor, uzi, Vibe Kanban: a human moves cards or presses keys. No orchestration logic at all.

dimensions.dimension: Is the workflow reviewable, versioned, diffable
dimensions.weft: It is a `.ts` file in `.weft/workflows/`. It goes through code review, `git blame` works on it, and `weft check` gates it (11 AST rules plus a best-effort `tsc` pass) before a run spends anything.

others.note: Specs, plans and task lists are checked-in markdown — the whole method is that they are reviewed artifacts.
Both the source markdown and the compiled `.lock.yml` are committed, so a reviewer sees exactly what CI will run.
A YAML file in the repo, parameterised and shareable.
Skills, commands and subagent definitions are files, distributable as plugins through a marketplace.
Agent definitions and rules are all committed files.
The script is model-authored per task and essentially disposable. Nothing is reviewed except the phase list, in the moment.
There is no workflow artifact to review.

dimensions.weft: `runWorkflow` drives the workflow to a terminal state on a private in-memory engine; `mock().on({ key }, responder)` fixtures pass through the engine's NORMAL schema validation and journaling — a fixture that would not pass in production fails the test. `exec`, `bash`, `fetch`, `env` and `answers` fixtures included, so a workflow with human steps and shell checks runs end to end in CI.

others.note: The strongest EVALUATION story anywhere — SWE-bench, SWE-smith, a stable trajectory format — but that is benchmark measurement, not unit testing, and it spends tokens.
Explicitly no offline or mocked execution mode. Every workflow run spends tokens.
No mocked-run mode; `retry.checks` verify the OUTPUT of a real run.
`gh aw compile` validates the workflow's shape, not its behaviour.
The SDK makes programmatic driving possible — the raw material for a harness — but nothing is published.
Conventional pytest plus benchmark harnesses; no published zero-model-call replay.

others.project: Spec Kit / opencode / Codex CLI / Aider / PR-Agent
others.note: No harness in any of them.

dimensions.weft: `schema` is REQUIRED on every `agent` and `human.*` call and on workflow I/O. The provider returns raw; the ENGINE validates against the real Standard Schema and, on failure, calls `provider.repair()` in the SAME session with the validation errors, up to `limits.repair`. A `z.string()` field is still prose — the guarantee is that what flows BETWEEN steps has a shape you declared.

others.note: `agent(prompt, { schema })` resolves to a parsed object validated at the tool-call layer — the closest thing to weft here. But there is no documented repair loop: it resolves to `null` on failure and the caller does `.filter(Boolean)`, which erases the reason.
`response.json_schema` enforces structured output for the WHOLE RUN — the same instinct, arrived at independently, but one schema at the boundary rather than a contract between steps.
JSON-based prompting produces structured findings the tool then renders; the contract is internal to the product, not something you compose against.
Tool-call schemas validated per the provider's function-calling contract, with retry on malformed XML. No typed step-result contract across a workflow.
Subagent results return to the main thread as SUMMARIES; no structured output contract for a subagent.
Tool schemas validated per provider; step-level structured output is not a documented primitive.
Pydantic models validate the EVENT envelope and tool arguments — not 'this step must return a value of this shape'.
Edits are validated structurally by edit format with retry on malformed diffs. That validates the DIFF, not a step result.
The unit is the action, not the step result.
Specs, plans and tasks are prose markdown all the way down. The hand-off between phases is a document.
No workflow layer, so nothing to type.

dimensions.weft: **None.** A weft write step hands an agent a fresh worktree stripped of the conventions every other runner in the ecosystem reads by default. `ctx.fs.read` exists, so a workflow author can pass conventions in by hand, but nothing does it for you and no example does it.

others.note: CLAUDE.md at every level, plus skills, plus output styles.
AGENTS.md — the convention Codex popularised and now shared across vendors.
GEMINI.md and AGENTS.md.
`.clinerules` for coding standards and architecture constraints.
Reads repository `AGENTS.md` files and `SKILL.md` definitions to steer review.
`/speckit.constitution` makes project principles an explicit, versioned input to every later phase.
Rules files, `.goosehints`, and Aider's tree-sitter repo-map respectively — different mechanisms, same job.
The markdown body is where conventions go, and the repo is right there.

dimensions.weft: A write step gets a PER-ATTEMPT worktree at `tmpdir/weft-worktrees/<runId>/<seq>.<attempt>`, seeded from `integrationBaseCommit` — a dangling-ref-pinned commit of the current tracked+untracked tree — so later writers build on earlier `ctx.integrate()` results rather than on HEAD.

others.note: The best in the field: DUAL isolation — a git worktree/branch for the code AND a Dagger container for the process, so installs, daemons, ports and env mutations are discarded with the step. The hole every worktree-only tool leaves open.
Worktree per subagent PLUS an OS sandbox (Seatbelt/Landlock/WFP), with `.git` protected even in workspace-write mode.
`claude --worktree <name>` on branch `worktree-<name>`, with base controlled by `worktree.baseRef`. Enforced, not advisory.
claude-squad, Crystal, Conductor, uzi, Vibe Kanban — worktree + branch per agent is literally the product; uzi also allocates per-agent dev-server ports.
Docker container per instance via SWE-ReX, each with its own checkout; output is a unified diff per instance.
Workspace as an abstraction — local, Docker, Kubernetes or remote — with ephemeral per-agent workspaces.
Worktree + branch per workspace with an experimental container backend, plus Pairing Mode syncing isolated work back to the local checkout.
Shadow-git checkpoints isolate HISTORY, not the tree — team specialists share `cwd`, so parallel members can clobber each other.
Operate directly on the working tree.

dimensions.weft: `write: { paths: [...], also: [...], mode: 'warn' | 'strict' }` makes a step a write step. On Claude the scope is enforced LIVE through `canUseTool` — scope-matched edits, symlink-escape realpath checks, a read-only bash allow-list, traversal and shared-git-metadata denial — and post-hoc by partitioning the captured patch, with `strict` quarantining an out-of-scope patch. **Asymmetric:** Codex has no permission hook, so there `strict` means post-hoc diffing only.

others.note: Structurally rather than by policy: the agent job holds NO write credentials, and can only emit schema-validated 'safe outputs' that a separate, differently-privileged job applies. A compromised agent cannot write.
`fileRegex` write restrictions per custom mode — a mode could be forbidden from touching anything but `*.md`. The closest prior art for path-scoped writes, and the project archived 2026-05.
Per-agent permission map over read / edit / bash / glob / grep / task, each `allow | ask | deny`. Capability-level, not path-level.
`sandbox_mode` confines writes to the workspace with `.git` protected — coarse-grained, and uniform across subagents.
Statically blocks edits into the main checkout when running in a worktree, and screens Bash for escapes. A screen, not a path-scope declaration.
No path scoping.

dimensions.weft: It does not, until you say so. A write step returns a PATCH blob; out-of-scope files are flagged or quarantined; nothing touches the integration tree until `ctx.integrate()`, which is itself a journaled step with `onConflict: 'ask' | 'fail' | 'agent'` and returns a ledger. **A run that ends with un-integrated, un-discarded patches fails.** What weft does NOT do: open a pull request.

others.note: Safe outputs include `create-pull-request` and `push-to-branch`, applied by a separate job. The change lands where review already happens.

others.project: Copilot coding agent / Codex Cloud / Jules
others.note: A pull request is the unit of delivery and the review surface, on the largest installed bases in the category.
Land as review comments and committable suggestions on an existing PR — the whole product is the last mile weft skips.
Built-in review UI with PR creation from the workspace.
A branch, and a human merges it. `cu diff` / `cu merge` / `cu apply` are good verbs, but there is no policy and no ledger.
Every edit is an auto-commit with a sensible message and `/undo` reverts — the strongest git INTEGRATION and the weakest isolation.
Edits land in the working tree as they happen.

dimensions.weft: `ctx.check(name, { exec: ['pnpm','test'], required: true })` is a journaled step returning `{ status, evidence }`; a failing REQUIRED check gates the run's completion. Checks are free — they are shell, not a paid subagent turn.

others.note: `retry { max_retries, checks }` where checks are shell commands validating the run's output — declarative success criteria, and the closest peer to `ctx.check`.
`--test-cmd` and `--lint-cmd` run after every change and feed failures back for automatic fixing. The tightest edit→verify loop in the field.
It is a GitHub Actions job: the rest of the pipeline is right there, and a failing job blocks the safe-output apply.
Tests decide the benchmark score, but they are the harness around the agent, not a gate inside its loop.
Run tests by spending a subagent turn; the documented 'run tsc until it passes' pattern pays a model call every round. No engine-level gate.
Running tests is something the agent may choose to do, not something that gates anything.

dimensions.dimension: Built-in review patterns (find→refute, judge panel, best-of-N)
dimensions.weft: `@techery/weft-stdlib` ships `adversarialVerify` (strict majority so an even panel does not kill on a tie), `judgePanel` (best-votes with a mean-score tiebreak, judge schema pinned to the attempt count), `loopUntilDry`, `completenessCritic` and `multiModalSweep` — as ordinary keyed steps, so they replay and test like anything else. **Unproven:** weft publishes no precision number for any of them.

others.note: Multi-agent architecture with specialised reviewers running simultaneously rather than one generalist pass — and a published F1 of 60.1% across eight tools in its own February 2026 benchmark.
AI layered over 40+ bundled deterministic linters and SAST scanners; topped Martian's independent 2026 benchmark at 51.2% F1 with the broadest platform coverage.
Indexes the entire codebase before commenting on a diff — a different bet (whole-repo context over panel structure) with 82% bug-catch claimed in its own July 2025 test.
`/code-review` and ultrareview are agentic review passes with real structure, but they are commands, not composable patterns you build a workflow from.
The research lineage that established find-then-verify — as benchmark methodology rather than a shipped library.

others.project: goose / Cline / opencode / Codex CLI / Aider
others.note: Review is whatever you prompt for.

dimensions.weft: One option on one step: `ctx.agent(prompt, { provider: 'codex', ... })`. A cross-vendor refutation panel is a per-step routing choice, and the engine — not the vendor — validates what comes back. **Caveat:** only `claude`, `codex` and `mock` exist, the built-in price table is Claude-only, and `strict` scopes mean different things per provider.

others.note: Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, 200+ via OpenRouter, Bedrock, Vertex, Ollama/LM Studio, with per-mode and per-specialist model selection.
Models.dev-backed catalogue with OAuth flows and per-agent overrides — the strongest genuinely model-agnostic story in the field.
A superset: LiteLLM for models, and Agent Client Protocol so whole third-party AGENTS (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI) are pluggable.
Architect/editor split is real per-role routing with a demonstrated cost/quality win — an expensive model plans, a cheap one applies.
GPT, Claude (incl. Opus 5), Gemini, DeepSeek, Mistral, plus LiteLLM for Bedrock/Vertex/Ollama/OpenRouter.
Copilot, Claude and Codex agents under one control plane with one review surface.
Copilot, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini and Pi — selected in frontmatter, per workflow rather than per step.
Per-subagent routing, but strictly inside the Anthropic family.
Per-subagent model AND reasoning effort, but OpenAI models only.

dimensions.weft: `ctx.gate` and `ctx.human.ask/approve/review` suspend the run DURABLY. The answer can arrive hours later from the CLI, the web UI, or the session that started the run, and is validated against the step's schema; a bad answer journals `human.rejected` and REOPENS the request rather than failing the run. Provenance is recorded: `answeredBy: human | policy | timeout`.

others.note: The best-designed in-process gating: `AlwaysConfirm()` / `NeverConfirm()` / `ConfirmRisky()` as first-class policy objects. In-process — kill it and the pending confirmation is gone.
The best per-action approval UX anywhere: Plan mode explores and asks before Act mode touches anything, every edit and command surfaces with a diff. In-process.
`approval_policy` with untrusted / on-request / never. In-process.
Per-agent `allow | ask | deny` maps — declarative and fine-grained, still in-process.
Review-and-commit UIs with inline diff commenting — approval AFTER the work, which is a deliberate and defensible different bet.
Explicitly review-after rather than approve-during: let the agent run fully isolated, then `cu diff`.
Documented: 'No mid-run user input. Only agent permission prompts can pause a run.' Multi-stage sign-off means splitting into separate workflows.
No blocking gate; safety is structural instead.

dimensions.weft: `Budget.charge` propagates up the parent chain; `remainingTokens`/`remainingUsd` take `min(own, ancestor headroom)`; a run tree shares one ceiling and `reserveCall` PARKS rather than refusing when a lane would overrun. A USD-only ceiling with a provider that reports no cost and has no configured price REFUSES the dispatch rather than charging $0 silently.

others.note: `--agent.model.per_instance_cost_limit` genuinely stops an instance, hardened across thousands of benchmark runs. Per-instance and total, but no parent/child inheritance.
`max_turns` is an enforced structural cap on iterations — not a spend ceiling.
Reasoning-effort tiers, cheaper model variants, and a concurrency cap on subagents. Structural levers, not a ceiling.
A cost ARCHITECTURE rather than a cap: subtasks return summaries not transcripts, keeping the orchestrator's context small.
Documented as advisory: past 25 scheduled agents or 1.5M projected tokens, 'the warning does not pause or limit the run'.
Detailed per-task token and USD accounting, zero enforcement. They tell you after you spent it.

dimensions.dimension: Does a long task survive the session (the instrument)
dimensions.weft: Every step is journaled; a resume re-executes the workflow body and serves completed steps from the journal, matching by CONTENT so editing the script between runs is tolerated. This is plumbing, not the product — it earns its keep exactly when a workflow is long enough or blocked long enough to outlive the session that started it, which is the case for an overnight audit or a gate waiting on a person.

others.project: Codex Cloud / Copilot coding agent / Jules
others.note: Server-side execution: the task survives your laptop closing because it was never on your laptop.
A persistence directory per conversation with documented pause/resume — state restoration rather than replay, so no step-level salvage.
`task-board.json` / `mailbox.json` persist and survive restarts, but that is coordination state, not step results.
Explicit: 'If you exit Claude Code while a workflow is running, the next session starts the workflow fresh.' Transcripts are durable; workflow runs are not.

others.project: goose / Aider / opencode / Codex CLI / container-use
others.note: Kill the process and the work in flight is gone.

dimensions.dimension: Audit trail of what the agent actually did
dimensions.weft: The journal plus two generated records: `report.md` (Outcome / Changes / Checks / Ledger / Failures & drops / Remaining risk / Next step) and the live tree. `weft explain <run> <step>` shows one step's route, prompt, output, usage and attempts; `weft diff <a> <b>` compares two runs by keyed step output.

others.note: Every AI change is a git commit with a sensible message — the simplest and most durable audit trail in the field, and the reason people still reach for it.
Shadow-git repository committing a full tree snapshot after every tool use, giving file-level undo including untracked files.
`cu log` and `cu diff` per environment: a complete record of what each agent did, discardable by deleting a branch.
The trajectory format is a stable, publishable artifact — the reason its results are reproducible.
`/workflows` shows the phase tree, per-agent tokens and any agent's tool calls live, and can pause a run or restart one agent — a better CONTROL surface than weft's, over a less durable record.
A diff view per session, and that is the record.

dimensions.weft: Within one run: `ctx.parallel` / `ctx.pipeline` with a global semaphore at `min(16, cpus−2)` and a 4096-item fan-out cap. Across runs: nothing. Two runs sharing a working tree both stage and mutate the real tree at `rt.cwd`, and the ownership lease is per-RUN, not per-repo.

others.note: claude-squad, uzi, Vibe Kanban, Conductor, Crystal exist for exactly this: many agents on many tasks at once, a human as scheduler. uzi even broadcasts one instruction to every running agent.
16 concurrent (fewer on low-CPU), 1,000 agents per run, plus prompt-cache-aware stagger so a fan-out pays the system-prompt prefix once.
Mission control across web, VS Code and mobile for many concurrent agent tasks.
One environment per agent, unlimited in principle, each fully isolated.
Specialists run in parallel but share `cwd`, so throughput is bought with a clobbering risk.
One agent, one tree.

dimensions.dimension: Where it runs — and what that posture costs
dimensions.weft: **Local, on a developer's own machine, by design.** A CLI plus an MCP server so a Claude Code or Codex session can drive it, plus a loopback-only daemon serving a single-page UI. No server, no database, no account, no code leaving the machine, and the credentials used are the ones already sitting in the developer's shell. State is `<cwd>/.weft`. The costs are real and mostly unpaid: no repo-root discovery (running from a subdirectory silently targets a different, empty `.weft`), no blob GC, and no repo-level mutex, so two runs sharing a working tree is undefined behaviour.

others.project: Claude Code / Codex CLI / opencode / goose / Aider
others.note: The same posture and the bar weft is actually competing against for a developer's attention: one install, entirely local, nothing to operate. Several of them also offer a hosted mode, which weft deliberately does not.
Local by construction — a laptop, a repo, several agents.
A local CLI that bolts onto whichever agent you already run — the least infrastructure of anything here.

CI-native by construction, which is a genuinely different product: the workflow runs on GitHub's machines against GitHub's checkout, with no developer present. Better for scheduled and event-driven work, unavailable for the thing you want to watch.

others.project: Codex Cloud / Copilot coding agent / Jules
others.note: Hosted. The task survives your laptop closing because it was never on it — bought with sending the repo to a vendor and losing local tooling.
Runs both ways: a local CLI and Docker image, or GitHub Actions and webhooks. The clearest demonstration that local-first and CI need not be exclusive.
IDE-native, which is even closer to where the developer is than a terminal.

dimensions.weft: Design preview. Not on npm. Zero users. The engineering around it is real — 16 packages versioned together, a tag-driven release pipeline with `verify:packing` and `verify:install`, CI on node 22 and 24 — but nothing has shipped.

others.note: 131.2k stars, MIT, integrations for 30+ coding agents. The spec-driven method has become a named practice.
142.9k stars on the issue tracker; Agent Skills published as an open standard in Oct 2025 with official skill repos past 157k stars, a plugin system and a Skills marketplace launched April 2026.
201k stars, MIT, ~8M reported MAU (unverified).
53.4k stars and, uniquely, vendor-neutral Linux Foundation governance — a procurement advantage for a layer that brokers competing vendors.
12.7k stars, community-owned since April 2026 and reverted from AGPL-3.0 to Apache-2.0.
5k stars, MIT, GitHub Next — early but with the strongest possible distribution channel.
Worth naming: Flowise archived at 55.4k, Roo Code archived at 24.3k, Vibe Kanban sunsetting at 27.9k. Being right about the mechanism is not what decided those.
